analysis.one_liner: Boosts IRS funding to audit high earners and large corporations and raises penalties on their underpayments.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote and died in committee, so none of its roughly $100 billion in decade-long IRS funding was enacted through it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given the IRS tens of billions of dollars through fiscal 2031 to hire enforcement staff, replace outdated technology, and improve taxpayer services, with audit targets aimed at people making over $1 million and corporations with over $20 billion in assets. It also would have required banks to report account activity for high earners whose income isn't reported to the IRS by anyone else, and raised underpayment penalties to 40% for taxpayers making over $5 million. It never received a hearing or a vote and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary, compliant taxpayers benefit in two ways: the bill directs new money to taxpayer services (roughly $2.5 billion a year at its peak), meaning better help lines and assistance for everyday filers, and it shifts enforcement attention toward high-income people and big corporations, who currently face far less audit scrutiny relative to what they owe. The Treasury also gains if uncollected taxes are recovered.

how_it_helps.text: Sets escalating audit targets aimed at the top of the income scale: 50% of individual returns showing $10 million or more of income, 20% of returns between $1 million and $5 million, and 95% of corporations with more than $20 billion in assets.
Appropriates rising amounts for IRS enforcement each year through fiscal 2031, reaching $8.5 billion per year, to hire staff for those audits.
Puts $2.5 billion a year into the IRS taxpayer services account by 2025, which funds the assistance and customer service ordinary filers use.
Provides $1 billion a year through 2031 to replace the IRS's outdated technology and improve its ability to detect business-income fraud.

Requires banks to report total deposits and withdrawals for accounts of people with adjusted gross income of $400,000 or more who have income that no third party reports to the IRS, closing a visibility gap for unreported income, including income flowing through partnerships and S corporations.

Raises the accuracy-related underpayment penalty from a flat 20% to 30% for taxpayers with taxable income between $2 million and $5 million and 40% for those above $5 million, and directs the IRS to report to Congress on shifting audit resources toward high-income filers and on revenue lost to offshore evasion.

analysis.who_pays: High-income individuals and large corporations pay directly, through more frequent audits, a new bank-reporting requirement for unreported income, and underpayment penalties of up to 40% of what they short-paid. Banks bear the administrative cost of building the reporting systems. The public treasury initially bears the roughly $100 billion in appropriations unless recovered tax revenue offsets it.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, large corporations, and banks

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates about $100.5 billion over ten years (roughly $70 billion for enforcement, $20.5 billion for taxpayer services, and $10 billion for operations support) with no offsetting revenue provisions, so the deficit impact depends entirely on enforcement actually collecting more than it spends.

The audit targets are extremely ambitious relative to what the IRS has ever done, and the bill itself acknowledges the challenge by requiring a plan to recruit and retain auditors with the specialized skills needed to examine high-income returns; missing those targets would leave the appropriations without the intended revenue payoff.

The new bank-reporting requirement obliges financial institutions to build systems that transmit account inflows and outflows for covered taxpayers, creating real compliance costs and handling sensitive financial data, although the bill limits it to accounts the IRS specifically identifies rather than all accounts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall almost entirely on taxpayers who are not reporting income they owe tax on, plus routine bank paperwork, which is the point of the bill. The honest concerns are fiscal and practical: the appropriations are front-loaded with no offsets, and the audit targets are far beyond the IRS's current or historical capacity, so the payoff depends on the agency actually hiring and retaining thousands of specialized auditors. As designed, the burden on ordinary filers is minimal and they gain services and a fairer enforcement mix.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the Stop CHEATERS Act on February 22, 2021.
Seven House Democrats signed on as cosponsors; no Republican did.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day it was introduced, and the committee took no further action on it.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate action ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income individuals and large corporations are better off because the bill died: they face no new audit targets, no bank reporting of previously unreported income, and no penalties of up to 40% on underpayments. Banks also avoid the cost of building the new reporting systems.

for.name: Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and set audit targets and penalty increases aimed at high-income people and large corporations.

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup; it stayed in committee from referral in February 2021 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsor and all seven cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill never advanced past a committee referral, so no recorded opposition exists.

industries.note: The bill would have required audits of 95% of corporations with more than $20 billion in assets, a dramatic expansion over current rates, plus higher penalties on underpayments. Stopping the bill preserves the current low-audit status quo.

Audit targets of 20% to 50% for returns over $1 million, bank reporting of accounts with unreported income for those over $400,000, and underpayment penalties of up to 40% all fall on this group. Their interest in blocking the bill runs against the interest of compliant taxpayers who bear the missing revenue.

Banks would have had to report total deposits and withdrawals for accounts the IRS identifies as belonging to covered high earners, requiring new systems and ongoing compliance work. The burden serves tax transparency rather than the banks' own interests.
Entities in which a $400,000-plus individual holds an ownership interest would have been covered by the new bank reporting, targeting business income that currently escapes third-party reporting.
